name: System Design & APIs
description: Stateless services, idempotency, caching, queues and the API contracts that survive production traffic.

modules.title: API Contracts
content: REST asks that each request carry everything needed to process it, so servers can scale horizontally without sticky sessions. The consequence is operational rather than philosophical: because no instance remembers the previous request, a balancer may send the next one anywhere, and an instance that dies can be replaced without replaying anything. The state still has to live somewhere, and the three candidate homes are a client-held token, a shared store such as a database or cache, and the request body itself. Trouble begins when a team keeps conversation state in process memory because it was convenient, which quietly pins a user to one instance and turns every rolling deploy into a wave of expired sessions. Once state is external, the same property is what lets you autoscale, shard and retry without asking which machine answered first.

Idempotency keys let a payment or order endpoint recognize retries. The server stores the key with the original result and returns that result instead of charging twice. The key is generated by the client and must survive the client crashing, so it belongs to the user action rather than to one HTTP request, and the server keeps it at least as long as the longest retry schedule a caller might plausibly use. Two subtleties cause most of the bugs: a retry that arrives while the original is still executing needs a lock or an explicit conflict response rather than a second side effect, and a request presenting a known key with a different body must be refused, because answering with the first result silently discards a real change. Storage is a unique index rather than a cache entry, since an evictable key is a double charge waiting to happen.

Cursor pagination keyset paginates on an indexed sort column, which stays stable when rows are inserted; offset pagination can skip or duplicate rows under writes. The cursor is an opaque token carrying the last seen sort values, so the next query becomes a seek on the index instead of counting and discarding, which is why deep pages stop degrading linearly. Two design consequences follow. The sort must be backed by an index the planner can actually use, and if the sort column is not unique the cursor needs a tiebreaker such as the primary key, because rows sharing a timestamp disappear between pages. Making the token opaque and signed matters too: an exposed numeric offset invites callers to page into regions you never intended to serve and turns pagination into a scraping tool.

Versioning an API is a statement about who is allowed to change what and when, which is why the great versioning debate is mostly misframed. Adding an optional request field or an extra response field is usually compatible; deleting a field, renaming one, tightening validation, changing which value a field means, or turning a nullable field into a required one are not, and some client you have never met depends on all of them. The practical mechanism is parallel change: publish the new shape, run both, migrate callers, then retire the old one on a schedule you can prove from traffic. A number in the URL does not by itself make a change safe, because a client pinned to v2 still breaks when v2 semantics drift, and a version header complicates caching and support. Versionless evolution works only when someone owns the list of consumers and reads it.

The error contract is the part of an API that clients code against most tightly and design least carefully. The status carries the class of problem; a stable machine-readable code carries what the client should do next, which in practice means retry, correct this field, or stop and file a bug. Free text is for humans and changes with copy edits, so logic keyed on a message string breaks during a marketing review. A validation failure should list every field that failed and why rather than the first reason only, because a form cannot redisplay eight errors one request at a time. The trap is an error response that is too helpful: echoing the rejected secret, naming which fields exist, or including a stack trace turns a debugging aid into an information leak and a support queue.

Consumer-driven contract testing replaces a shared assumption about what an endpoint returns with an executable promise. The consumer declares the interactions it genuinely uses, the provider replays those declarations against itself in CI, and a change that drops a field or renames a verb fails a build instead of a dashboard. It catches the defect class that integration tests miss, which is a provider passing its own suite while quietly removing something no provider test asserted. It does not catch semantic drift, a slow dependency, or a consumer whose code ignored the contract, so a team treating contracts as complete coverage ships the same outages with more files. Boundary validation, generated typed clients and a lint against unknown fields are what keep the promise honest between releases.

Rate limits belong to the contract, so they need a documented unit, a documented identity and a documented rejection. A per-source-IP limit punishes everyone behind one corporate NAT or carrier gateway and is close to useless for a public API, while a per-key limit lets you describe a caller's behaviour, price it, and revoke one abuser without collateral damage. A limit enforced in each process is approximate once the fleet scales, because a local counter multiplies your advertised ceiling by the instance count, so the shared counter has to be small, fast and degradable. The rejection then has to say how long to wait and which limit was hit: a silent drop or a generic server error converts a designed backpressure signal into a retry storm, which is the one failure mode a rate limiter was supposed to prevent.

modules.title: Scale and Failure
content: Caching reduces latency but introduces staleness. TTL jitter, request coalescing and stale-while-revalidate reduce cache stampedes when a hot key expires. Each of those answers a different question, which is why grabbing one at random fails: jitter spreads expirations so a warm-up wave does not collapse into a single synchronized moment, coalescing lets one reader pay for a reload while the rest wait briefly on the same result, and stale-while-revalidate trades a latency spike for a documented window of wrongness. The correctness argument is the one teams lose, because a cached price, permission or inventory count is a business fact served late rather than a performance detail, so expiry policy is written per endpoint and not applied as a global default that nobody re-reads after the first incident.

Queues decouple producers from consumers and absorb bursts, at the cost of eventual consistency, duplicate delivery and the need for idempotent consumers. The decoupling is the point: a producer that cannot reach a slow dependency keeps working, and capacity is added by widening the drain instead of the funnel. The cost arrives as a lag number nobody owned, because an unbounded queue converts a throughput problem into a latency problem that only users notice, and a consumer killed halfway through means work is either resumable or repeated. Scaling follows queue depth rather than processor usage, so an autoscaler watching CPU reacts long after the backlog formed. The handler is where the guarantee is actually produced, since a broker can only promise to try again.

Observability combines metrics, structured logs and distributed traces so failures can be localized instead of guessed at. The three answer different questions and are priced differently: metrics aggregate cheaply and say that something is wrong now, logs retain the detail of one request and grow with cardinality, traces show which hop in a fan-out consumed the time. A dashboard of averages detects a steady degradation and misses a tail, while logs without a correlation id hand you ten thousand unrelated error lines and no way to group them per request. The failure to design for is the one you have never seen, which is why the metric set stays small, the sampling decision keeps slow and failed requests, and every alert names the check a human can actually run.

Load, throughput and utilization are three different quantities, and conflating them causes most capacity arguments. Load is the demand arriving; throughput is completed work per unit time; utilization is the fraction of time a resource is busy. A saturated resource keeps utilization near its ceiling while throughput stops rising and the queue grows, which is why a busy-but-healthy dashboard and a busy-and-dying one look identical until latency is plotted against utilization rather than against time. Waiting time grows superlinearly as utilization approaches one, and much worse when arrivals are bursty or service times vary, so a server that behaves at a high percentage under a smooth synthetic test becomes unbearable at the same percentage under real traffic. The number to publish alongside any utilization figure is the latency measured at it.

Tail latency is a property of concurrency rather than of individual requests, and it is why wide fan-out services feel slower than their averages suggest. A page that asks forty backends and waits for all of them has a latency equal to the maximum of forty samples, so a rare slow node becomes a common slow page, and the slowness comes from ordinary sources: a collection pause, a lock holder descheduled, a cold cache, a noisy neighbour, a shard mid-migration. Retries make it worse because they add load precisely when capacity is gone, and a timeout that is too long to abandon a slow peer keeps the pool occupied for the whole unlucky duration. Attacking the tail therefore means attacking variance with bounded per-dependency pools, short deadlines, hedged attempts for read-only fan-out, and capacity headroom sized for the recovery burst rather than the mean.

Scaling a system is a sequence of bottleneck handoffs, and the honest diagram is a queue of constraints rather than a graph of services. Removing state from process memory makes the web tier elastic, which moves pressure to the database; reads spread to replicas, and writes eventually meet a single-writer ceiling that no quantity of application instances relieves. That is why one workload scales by adding servers and another does not: a request whose cost is per-item is embarrassingly parallel, while a request that serializes on one row, one counter, one globally ordered partition or one hot key has a ceiling set by that object's throughput. The scaling plan should name the next bottleneck and the move for it, because the alternative is discovering it during the event you were preparing for and spending the incident on a rewrite.

Graceful degradation is a priority list written down and enforced in code, because a loaded system sheds something whether or not you chose what. Load shedding rejects work early, cheaply and in proportion, protecting queues and pools for the requests that still matter; without it every request slow-fails together and the whole service loses to a smaller one that dropped low-value traffic first. Failover adds a second tax: the moment capacity moves, caches are cold, pools are empty, replication is behind and every client reconnects at once, so the healthy machine inherits a burst larger than the one that triggered the failover. Sizing for steady state plus one node turns that into a failover that degrades the cluster instead of surviving it, which is why drills measure the recovery shape rather than the switch.

modules.title: Caching, Queues and Asynchronous Work
content: Deciding that work happens later is a product decision disguised as an architecture decision, because the experience must answer one simple question: what is the status now? A synchronous call reports failure inside the response, while a queue reports failure by not finishing, so an accepted request needs a resource the client can poll or a callback the client can trust, and both need their own contract. The right asynchronous candidates are steps whose latency the user does not experience as a decision, such as mail, thumbnails, search indexing, invoice rendering and analytics, whereas authorizing a payment or reserving stock is a user-visible fact that belongs on the request path with a strict deadline. The usual regret is putting the authoritative write behind a queue and then inventing a compensating flow for the user who refreshes too early.

Delivery guarantees describe the broker rather than the outcome, and the gap between the two is where double charges live. Most brokers persist a message before acknowledging the producer and remove it after the consumer reports completion, so a consumer that dies in between receives it again, while a broker that deletes before the consumer commits loses it instead. At-least-once is the survivable default because duplicates can be absorbed by a deduplication record written in the same transaction as the business change; at-most-once silently loses work, and exactly-once across a broker and a database would require a distributed transaction committing to two logs that no engine actually shares. The phrase worth designing for is exactly-once processing, which is what at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent handler actually produces.

A queue's ordering guarantee is defined by its unit of parallelism, and the mismatch between the two is the usual cause of lost updates. A broker that preserves order only within a partition lets you choose the grouping key, so events for one aggregate are keyed by its identifier and stay ordered while unrelated aggregates are handled concurrently by the rest of the fleet. Hashing that key spreads load unevenly the moment one tenant is busy, which is where the throughput ceiling really sits: the fleet idles while one partition drains. Teams that require total order across everything discover it costs the throughput of a single consumer, at which point the cheaper answer is usually to make handlers order-insensitive with sequence numbers or version checks rather than buying a bus that serializes the world.

Publishing an event and updating a row are two writes, and the space between them is a crash window. A handler that commits and then publishes can fail in the gap and leave state that no subscriber will ever hear about; publishing first announces a fact about a transaction that then rolls back. A transactional outbox closes the gap by writing the event inside the same database transaction as the state change, so the pair becomes one atomic unit, and a relay publishes outbox rows with at-least-once semantics, which still obliges subscribers to deduplicate. The outbox needs size discipline as well, because a relay stuck during an incident accumulates rows in the table that also holds your live data and turns a lag into a storage emergency. Change data capture is the same idea lifted into the write log: cheaper to operate at volume, harder to reason about.

Asynchronous work turns error handling into a retention policy. A synchronous failure is visible to the caller and then gone; a poisoned message is retried forever unless attempts are bounded, and one that is retried while holding a partition blocks everything behind it, which is an outage dressed up as a bug. A dead-letter queue exists to move the failing message off the critical path with its attempt count, error text and original arrival time attached so a human can reason about it later, and it earns its place only if something alerts on that queue's depth and something else replays it after a fix. Replaying into an unchanged dependency recreates the incident, and replaying out of order can write an old state over a new one, which is the second reason handlers should compare versions before applying.

Backpressure is the mechanism that stops a pipeline from turning an incident into an outage, and it is nearly always the last thing designed. A producer that never blocks, a queue that never refuses and a consumer that never slows down all assume somebody downstream will absorb the difference, and the component that actually absorbs it is the broker's memory or disk. The working controls are bounded queues that refuse with a counted reason, producers that see the refusal and shed or fail visibly, and consumers that stop prefetching once their unfinished work hits a limit. Losing a low-value telemetry message under load is a correct outcome; holding everything until the broker runs out of space and takes the payment topic with it is the outcome that gets written up. Shedding rules belong in documentation, because silence and success look identical in metrics.

Timers and scheduled jobs inside a fleet need a leader, and teams remember this when two replicas send the same reminder. A per-instance scheduler runs once per process, so scaling out multiplies scheduled work, while a single dedicated scheduler becomes the component nobody failovers. The durable answer is a lease: a job claims a row or key with an expiry, works while holding it, and lets the expiry release the claim if the process dies, which yields at-least-once execution and makes idempotency mandatory rather than optional. Long jobs need heartbeats so a slow worker is not reassigned mid-flight, and reassigned work needs a fencing token so the zombie's write cannot clobber the new owner's result. The same arithmetic bites retry schedules that all wake on the same wall-clock second and arrive together.

modules.title: Data Modeling, Sharding and Store Choice
content: A service boundary is real where the data changes together and ownership is single. Two services reading and writing one table is not a distributed architecture but a monolith with a shared schema and a network in the middle, because every column rename needs both teams deploying in the right order and every tuning decision becomes a negotiation. Ownership means one writer, an explicit interface for everything else, and deliberate duplication where another service cannot afford a synchronous call for a fact it needs. Duplication is a decision with a price rather than a sin: the copy needs a refresh path, its staleness has to be tolerable to the feature reading it, and divergence is a bug class that no test suite catches cheaply. The question that settles most arguments is who gets paged when this data is wrong.

Shard keys are chosen for the queries you run most and the writes you cannot batch, which is why the decision reads as a bet on the future. High cardinality and an even arrival pattern spread writes; a key that appears in most read filters lets a query target one shard rather than broadcasting to all of them, and a broadcast multiplies cost by cluster size while making ordering and limits awkward. Both aims collide when reads are per tenant and writes are per device event, and the resolutions are a composite key, a derived bucket that mixes tenant with a hashed suffix to break hot spots, or a second copy of the data indexed the other way. The advice gets repeated because changing the key afterwards means copying a live dataset while it keeps serving traffic.

A hot shard is a key-design failure rather than a capacity problem, which is why adding nodes does not help. A single large tenant, a status field used as the partition key, a date bucket during a promotion or a globally ordered counter all concentrate load on one node while the rest of the cluster idles, and cluster-average dashboards look healthy while one disk and one thread saturate. Mitigations break the key apart: a counter spread over sub-keys and summed at read time, a hot identifier salted into buckets, or a bursty writer routed through a queue that drains at a controlled rate. A cache in front absorbs a hot read but does nothing for a hot write. The cheap diagnostic is reading load per shard rather than per cluster early enough that the pattern is visible before the node is out of options.

Choosing a primary key in a distributed system trades locality against coordination. A monotonic sequence gives compact indexes, ordered scans and cheap pagination, but every insert lands on the leading edge of the same structure, which is a hotspot by construction and a contention point under high write rates, and it leaks business volume to anyone who can read an identifier. A random identifier spreads inserts across the tree and lets any node generate values without asking anyone, at the cost of worse cache locality, larger secondary indexes and no natural ordering, which is why an identifier with a time prefix is the common compromise. Whichever you choose, a guessable integer across tenants is an authorization question, so access control belongs on the row rather than on the unguessability of a number.

Read models and projections exist because the write model is normalized for integrity and useless for a screen. A dashboard needing eight joins across three services is not a query but a batch job pretending to be one, so the sustainable design builds a denormalized document as events arrive and serves the page from a store shaped like the page itself. The cost is a second pipeline with its own lag, its own defects and its own backfill story: whenever projection logic changes, someone rebuilds history while live writes continue, and that rebuild must order by event sequence rather than wall-clock time or it will overwrite newer state with older. CQRS names the split between command and query models without demanding separate databases, and the gap between them has to surface in the interface as pending rather than as silently wrong.

Schema evolution across a boundary is a sequencing problem, because deployment and rollback stop being symmetric once data is involved. Adding a nullable column or an optional field is safe; renaming one is a two-step expand then contract, where the new name is written, both names are read, history is backfilled in batches small enough to leave the primary responsive, and only then does the old name stop being produced. Dropping the old column is the last step and requires proof from traffic rather than a code search, since consumers you do not know about read what you no longer grep for. The accident people actually have is a rollback landing after rows were written in the new shape, which the old code cannot read; dual-read tolerance and a version field on the row are cheap insurance against it.

Store selection is a list of constraints rather than a league table, and the first constraint is usually operational rather than functional. A relational engine gives you joins, constraints, transactions and twenty years of operators who can run it, which covers a startling number of products, and the honest reason to add a second engine is a query it genuinely cannot serve: relevance-ranked text, an unbounded hierarchy, a high-cardinality counter, similarity search, or a working set that must live in memory. Each extra engine costs a pipeline, a backup story, an on-call surface and a consistency question, and estates almost never shrink afterwards. The pattern that survives review keeps a boring primary as the source of truth with derived stores fed from its change log, because a broken derived index is then rebuildable rather than unrecoverable.

modules.title: Resilience: Timeouts, Retries, Circuit Breakers and Idempotency
content: A timeout is a budget, and it should be set from the caller's deadline rather than from the dependency's happy path. Every unbounded call converts someone else's slowness into your stuck worker, because the thread, the connection and the pool slot stay held while the remote side takes whatever it takes, so a service that depends on unbounded calls has an outage whose duration is decided by another team. Deadlines propagate by carrying the remaining time downstream and letting each hop refuse work it cannot finish, which stops a request the client already abandoned from burning capacity at the fifth level of a call graph. The value itself comes from measurement plus headroom, and a timeout shorter than the natural work it covers simply manufactures failures, which is the outcome people then blame on the mechanism.

Retries turn a failure rate into a load multiplier, and the arithmetic is unforgiving. If every client retries once after a timeout, a dependency failing at a tenth of requests receives roughly its normal volume again as second attempts, and because failing requests are the slow ones, that extra traffic lands while capacity is already gone. Exponential backoff without jitter still synchronizes a fleet that failed at the same instant, so the pieces that actually bound amplification are randomization and a retry budget, a cap on what fraction of calls may be retries at all. Retrying must also be restricted to operations safe to repeat: a bounded read is harmless, a create without an idempotency key is a duplicate-order generator, and retrying a response you received but could not parse is a logic bug wearing a transient-failure costume.

A circuit breaker exists to stop paying a dependency's latency tax when it cannot serve, not to heal it. Tripping on a failure threshold makes calls fail immediately, which keeps caller threads and pools from being consumed by slow failures and gives the overloaded dependency a window that is not a continuous assault. The caller then has to decide what an open circuit means for a user: cached data, a reduced feature, an honest error, or a queued attempt. Half-open states release a small number of probes rather than the whole traffic, because a recovering node hit by a full reconnect storm looks broken again, and the flapping that follows is worse than the original failure. The classic misconfiguration is a breaker around a dependency every request needs with no fallback at all, which converts partial failure into total.

Bulkheads are about the cost of waiting rather than the count of errors. A service using one connection pool and one worker pool for everything shares a failure domain with every dependency, so one slow downstream call occupies capacity that an unrelated endpoint needed, and the visible symptom is a total outage caused by a partial one. Splitting pools per dependency bounds the damage: the sick dependency exhausts its own small pool while the rest of the service keeps answering. Sizing is the hard part, because pools large enough to isolate everything sum to more than the process can hold and you have rediscovered the original problem with extra configuration. Queue limits, concurrency caps and per-tenant ceilings are the same idea, each trading a little throughput for a failure that stays in one place instead of touring the building.

Fail fast and fail open are choices about which failure you prefer. An authorization or feature-flag dependency that has become unreachable can be treated as a denial, which protects correctness and produces an outage for genuine users, or as a permissive default, which keeps the site working and opens a window in which the missing check is the incident. The decision depends on what the check protects and how long it can plausibly be unavailable, and it needs an owner and a written rule, because a library default makes it accidentally. Fail-closed on a cache is the same question in different clothing, since a miss storm against a database sized for a hit ratio it no longer has is an outage by design. The option nobody argues for is the one most systems ship: a long timeout plus two retries deciding on the operator's behalf at three in the morning.

Idempotency is what makes repetition safe, and in a retried system repetition is not exceptional. It has to cover clients that resend, brokers that redeliver, load balancers that replay, humans who double-click and operators who replay a day of events, so a handler's safety cannot depend on any of them being polite. Server-side enforcement is a unique constraint rather than a check-then-write in memory, because two instances answering simultaneously both find nothing there; the key is scoped to the caller, and a known key presenting a different payload must be refused rather than answered from history. The response is the last piece, since a client retrying after a network cut cannot distinguish a duplicate from a fresh result unless the answer says so, and an ambiguous conflict costs more support time than the double charge it avoided.

Partial failure is the normal operating state of a distributed system, which makes health a per-signal question rather than a boolean. A process that accepts a connection may be unable to serve a request because its pools are drained or its queue is deep, so a check that only establishes connectivity declares a dying instance healthy; conversely a readiness check that asks every downstream dependency can turn one outage into everyone's outage by removing the whole fleet from rotation at once. The useful design separates running from able-to-serve, gives the platform a short grace period to finish in-flight work, and keeps dependency probes cheap, cached and rarely decisive. Flapping is what aggressive checks do relative to recovery time, and a fleet removed and restored repeatedly amplifies load on whatever remains.

modules.title: Capacity Planning, Observability and Cost
content: Capacity planning starts from a demand shape rather than a peak number, because the peak is a symptom of the shape. The quantities you need are arrival rate, cost per request, concurrency and the growth curve, and Little's law ties three of them together: the average number of in-flight requests equals arrival rate multiplied by average latency, so two hundred requests per second at a quarter of a second each keeps fifty requests resident continuously, and that is what pools, queues and connection limits must hold. The same relation gives headroom its form, since doubling traffic at unchanged latency doubles in-flight work, and a pool that fitted at one load stops fitting well before a utilization dashboard admits anything. Every capacity claim should therefore arrive with the concurrency and queue limits it was measured against.

A load test answers a question only when its arrival model matches production. A closed-loop test drives a fixed number of virtual users who wait for each response, so as the system slows, offered load quietly falls, and the run reports stable throughput with awful latency, which reads like a capacity ceiling and is really a concurrency artifact. An open-loop test issues at a planned rate regardless of responses and can find the point where the system stops keeping up, provided the generator itself is not the limit and the traffic carries realistic payload sizes, authentication work, cold versus warm cache mix and the seasonal endpoint blend. Synthetic tests against an empty cache and an idle database measure a system nobody operates, which is why benchmark numbers are so reliably wrong when a real event arrives.

Latency percentiles describe a distribution rather than a target, and misreading them is a durable career hazard. An average of one hundred and twenty milliseconds is compatible with ninety percent of requests finishing in forty and one percent taking seconds, and it is the tail that generates complaints, timeouts, retries and the load spike behind them. A percentile is only meaningful when the bucket contains enough traffic to be stable and when a request that timed out counts as slow instead of vanishing from the sample, which is a common instrumentation bug. Comparing your own percentile across time is useful; lifting a percentile from a blog post and calling it a goal is not, because distribution shape depends on fan-out, batch size, collection pauses and what your sampler chose to discard.

Traces show where time went and metrics show whether it mattered, and each carries a cost model that shapes what you learn. Recording every span for every request is unaffordable at volume, so head-based sampling decides before the outcome is known and therefore discards the slow and failed requests you most wanted, while tail-based sampling keeps those by deciding afterwards and needs a buffer of in-flight traces to do it. An exemplar linking a latency histogram to one trace is what turns a spike on a dashboard into an investigation, and a correlation id in the log line is what makes the trace findable afterwards. Cardinality is the trap: a label per user, request or path multiplies series, inflates the monitoring bill and can take down the store that fires the alerts.

Autoscaling is control on a delayed signal, and the delay is the interesting part. Scaling on processor utilization reacts after latency has already degraded, because a saturated dependency shows up as queueing before it shows as CPU, and a scale-out is not instantaneous since images pull, migrations run, caches warm and pools rebuild, so the fleet grows into the incident rather than ahead of it. Queue depth, in-flight concurrency or a schedule known in advance are leading signals, and asymmetric thresholds plus a cooldown stop a fleet oscillating around one workload. Every automated response still needs a human override, because an autoscaler reacting to a traffic drop caused by your own outage scales down at precisely the moment recovery needs the headroom, which is a self-inflicted second incident.

Alerting should fire on what users feel and on the causes that predict it, which is why a wall of red panels trains people to ignore all of it. Symptom alerts on failed requests or exhausted error allowance are often the only thing worth acting on at night, while cause alerts on a queue that will not drain or a volume that will fill buy time but must stay rare and specific enough that a person does something. Burn-rate style detection exists to catch both a fast collapse and a slow leak without spamming, and the honest review question for each rule is what a human does differently when it fires. An alert with no owner and no runbook is a notification, and a page requiring three dashboards before anyone can judge severity escalates to whoever has seen this particular shape before.

Cost becomes a design constraint because it multiplies with every other decision. A cache that removes a dependency call also adds an engine to operate, a pipeline to keep correct and a staleness bug to triage, so its value is measured in avoided work rather than in a latency number; a shard bought for headroom bills continuously for the spike that justified it, and the fleet that survives an event is the one you keep paying for afterwards. The measurement that changes behaviour is cost per unit of product rather than total spend, because it exposes a feature whose per-request work grew silently with each release and makes an engineer ask whether a report really needs to be real-time. Cross-region redundancy and durability tiers are the same argument at a larger scale.

questions.text: What does statelessness mean in REST?
questions.a: The server keeps per-client session state between requests
questions.b: Each request carries the information needed to process it
questions.c: Responses can only be cached when the server holds no state at all
questions.d: Session data must be written into the request body of every call
questions.explanation: State may live in the client, a database or a cache, but the server does not need per-client memory to answer a request. Option C confuses statelessness with cacheability, which depends on the response headers instead.

questions.text: Why use an idempotency key on a payment endpoint?
questions.a: It encrypts the payment payload
questions.b: It replaces authentication for the endpoint
questions.c: It lets the server recognize retries and avoid charging twice
questions.d: It guarantees lower latency by skipping the payment processor entirely
questions.explanation: The key maps to the first outcome; retries return that stored outcome instead of repeating the side effect. It is not a performance device, and it says nothing about encryption or authentication.

questions.text: What makes horizontal scaling straightforward?
questions.a: Sticky sessions must be enabled in every case
questions.b: Moving to a larger instance type on the same host achieves the same result
questions.c: Load balancing cannot be used while instances are stateless
questions.d: Stateless app servers that share external storage
questions.explanation: Any instance can serve any request, so the balancer is free to distribute traffic. Option B describes vertical scaling, which changes a ceiling rather than removing it.

questions.text: How does a token bucket rate limiter work?
questions.a: It blocks all bursts unconditionally
questions.b: It allows bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing an average rate
questions.c: It counts requests per user per month and resets on the first day of the month
questions.d: It is a database index
questions.explanation: Tokens refill at a steady rate; accumulated tokens permit short bursts without exceeding the long-term rate. Fixed calendar windows are a different algorithm and behave badly at the boundary.

questions.text: Which techniques reduce a cache stampede?
questions.a: Increasing TTL always fixes it
questions.b: It is caused by too much memory being allocated to the cache
questions.c: TTL jitter, request coalescing and stale-while-revalidate
questions.d: It only happens with Redis Cluster
questions.explanation: Spreading expirations, collapsing duplicate loads and serving stale data during refresh all reduce the thundering herd. A longer TTL only postpones the synchronized moment rather than removing it.

questions.text: Why is cursor pagination more stable than offset pagination?
questions.a: Offset pagination is always stable
questions.b: Cursors require sorting by primary key only, so they cannot use other custom indexes
questions.c: Cursor pagination cannot use indexes
questions.d: Cursors stay stable when rows change, while offsets can skip or duplicate rows
questions.explanation: Offsets are positions in a result set; inserts shift those positions. Cursors anchor to a value in the ordered index, which needs an index on the sort column but not necessarily one on the key.

questions.text: What is the main operational weakness of stateless JWTs?
questions.a: They never expire
questions.b: They cannot be individually revoked without a denylist or short expiry
questions.c: They are encrypted by default
questions.d: Deleting the browser cookie revokes them on the server on the next request
questions.explanation: Verification needs no server lookup, which is exactly why revocation requires extra infrastructure. Option D is the comforting mistake: the server never sees the deletion.

questions.text: What benefit does a message queue provide during a traffic spike?
questions.a: It makes every request synchronous
questions.b: Queues remove the need for idempotent consumers
questions.c: It decouples producers and consumers and buffers the spike
questions.d: It guarantees exactly-once delivery in every mainstream broker configuration
questions.explanation: Consumers drain at their own pace while the producer keeps working. Most brokers deliver at-least-once, so option B is the dangerous reading of the same feature.

questions.text: What trade-off comes with read replicas?
questions.a: They remove write bottlenecks
questions.b: They guarantee strong consistency
questions.c: They replace backups by keeping a full copy of every write
questions.d: They scale reads but introduce replication lag
questions.explanation: Reads may see stale data during lag, and replicas do not help the primary accept writes. Option C is a common operational error: a replica replicates deletions and corruption too.

questions.text: Why are metrics, logs and traces used together?
questions.a: Logs alone always suffice
questions.b: Metrics replace tracing
questions.c: Together they make distributed failures diagnosable
questions.d: Observability only means monitoring CPU, memory and disk usage
questions.explanation: Metrics detect symptoms, traces locate the slow hop and logs explain the specific error. Option D describes host monitoring, which cannot answer a question about one request crossing four services.

questions.text: What does versioning an API primarily protect?
questions.a: The promise that a client-side contract will not change underneath the caller
questions.b: A guarantee that the provider tested the new release
questions.c: A way of keeping old clients off new code paths so that responses get faster for everyone
questions.d: A requirement for using JSON instead of form encoding
questions.explanation: Versioning is a commitment about change, not a performance switch or a media-type rule. Option C is the tempting misconception that old code paths are dead weight rather than a live contract.

questions.text: An endpoint's response gains one additional field. Which consumer is most likely to break?
questions.a: A client that ignores fields it did not ask for
questions.b: A client configured to reject unknown fields at its deserialization boundary
questions.c: A client that caches responses and honours the cache headers received from that endpoint
questions.d: A client that authenticates every request with a bearer token
questions.explanation: Strict parsers that fail on unrecognized keys turn an additive change into an outage. Caching and authentication are unaffected by an extra field, which is why they read like plausible answers.

questions.text: Why can adding one new value to an enum field in a response be a breaking change?
questions.a: Because most JSON parsers fail the whole document when a string value is not in the allow list compiled into the client
questions.b: Because an enum is the one field type that cannot be made optional
questions.c: Because generated clients refuse to rebuild when the schema changes
questions.d: Because consumers often switch exhaustively over known values and have no default branch for a new one
questions.explanation: The danger is in consumer code that treats the known set as complete, so an unseen value falls through. Option A overstates parser behaviour: JSON itself accepts any string, which is why the bug reaches production.

questions.text: What is the practical reason to return a stable machine-readable error code alongside the status?
questions.a: Because status codes are far too few to name every business failure, so the custom code list quietly becomes the contract
questions.b: Because a code lets the client log something readable rather than show the message to the user
questions.c: Because clients branch on the code, while message text is rewritten without anyone calling that a breaking change
questions.d: Because a status code alone cannot carry a retry hint, which only an error body can supply
questions.explanation: Prose is edited freely and is not an interface, so behaviour has to hang on a code that is documented as stable. Option A is the trap: codes supplement the status class rather than replacing it.

questions.text: What does a published API schema, such as an OpenAPI document, actually give a team?
questions.a: Proof that the running implementation behaves exactly as the design document says it should, in every environment
questions.b: Something to generate typed clients from, validate requests against, and lint during review
questions.c: Automatic backward compatibility for every field that gets added later
questions.d: A mechanical replacement for contract tests between consumers and providers
questions.explanation: A schema is a tool for generation and validation, and it is only as true as whoever keeps it updated. Option A is the wish: nothing in the document forces the deployed code to match it.

questions.text: For a running service, what distinguishes load from throughput?
questions.a: They are two names for the same measurement of requests per second
questions.b: Throughput is the demand arriving, while load is the work actually completed
questions.c: Load is measured per request in milliseconds while throughput is measured per instance in megabytes of bandwidth
questions.d: Load is arriving demand, throughput is completed work, and utilization says how busy the resource is
questions.explanation: The three quantities diverge exactly when the system is in trouble, which is why conflating them ends arguments wrongly. Option B swaps the definitions, a common slip in capacity reviews.

questions.text: A service handles 200 requests per second and each takes about 250 milliseconds. How many requests are in flight?
questions.a: About fifty, since in-flight work equals arrival rate times average duration
questions.b: About two hundred, because every request holds a worker for its whole life
questions.c: About five, because the queue smooths bursts before they reach the workers
questions.d: It cannot be estimated at all without knowing how many processor cores sit behind the load balancer
questions.explanation: Little's law gives 200 times 0.25 seconds, so fifty requests are resident at any moment. Option D is the comfortable error: concurrency follows from rate and latency, not from core count.

questions.text: A dashboard reports average request latency of 120 milliseconds while users keep complaining. What does the average hide?
questions.a: That the service has a memory leak that inflates latency over time
questions.b: Whether the deployment is running more instances than the traffic justifies
questions.c: A distribution with most requests fast and a minority slow enough to time out and be retried
questions.d: Nothing, because the average is the standard way to describe tail behaviour in a latency histogram
questions.explanation: The mean weights the fast majority, so a small slow tail barely moves it while driving every timeout and retry. Option D is the misconception that keeps the dashboard unchanged after the complaints.

questions.text: A page waits on forty backends before rendering. Why does a rare slow backend produce a common slow page?
questions.a: Because the slowest backend also holds the largest share of the connection pool
questions.b: The page's latency is the maximum of forty samples, so a rare outlier appears often at that fan-out
questions.c: Because balancers round-robin and therefore cluster slow responses together
questions.d: Because all forty backends must sit in the same failure domain before a page can render successfully at all
questions.explanation: Waiting for the maximum of many samples pushes the page toward the tail of each backend, amplifying rare slowness. Option D sounds structural but confuses fan-out with a shared failure domain.

questions.text: Adding web servers does nothing for a workload in which every request takes a lock on the same account row. What does that show?
questions.a: The ceiling is the throughput of one object, so the design needs to break that object apart
questions.b: The database has to be vertically scaled to a much larger instance before application-level scaling means anything
questions.c: Read replicas are the correct fix, since the contention is purely a read-side phenomenon
questions.d: The balancer is misconfigured and sending too many requests to one instance
questions.explanation: Work that serializes on one key has a ceiling set by that key, so more instances only queue faster at the same wall. Option C is the trap: replicas help reads, and this is a write lock.

questions.text: What usually causes the latency spike that follows a database failover to a healthy replica?
questions.a: The new primary must replay the entire transaction log from the beginning before it is allowed to accept any traffic
questions.b: Clients wait for a fixed cooling period built into replication protocols
questions.c: The replica's indexes are rebuilt from scratch during promotion
questions.d: Cold caches, empty connection pools and a simultaneous reconnect storm hit the new primary at once
questions.explanation: Promotion moves capacity, not warm state, so the healthy node inherits a burst larger than the traffic that caused the failover. Option A misreads replication: a promoted replica already has the committed data.

questions.text: Which kind of work is the best candidate for an asynchronous path rather than the request path?
questions.a: Anything that currently requires a database transaction to complete correctly
questions.b: Any step whose result the user is actively waiting on before deciding what to do next in the interface
questions.c: Work that cannot be retried safely if the worker crashes halfway through
questions.d: Side effects the user does not experience as a decision, such as mail, thumbnails or indexing
questions.explanation: Deferring is safe when no user decision depends on the outcome, and it is exactly wrong when one does. Option C names the real prerequisite: if a retry is unsafe, the work is not ready to be asynchronous.

questions.text: A consumer processes a message and crashes just before acknowledging it. What does an at-least-once broker do?
questions.a: It redelivers the message, so the handler must recognize that the work already happened
questions.b: It discards the message outright, since a consumer that crashed mid-work is treated as a poison message
questions.c: It rolls the message back to the producer for a fresh send
questions.d: It replays only the uncommitted part of the handler's work from its own log
questions.explanation: Nothing was acknowledged, so the message returns and the handler must deduplicate against its own record of the work. Option D imagines the broker understands a transaction it cannot see inside.

questions.text: Why can a broker not honestly promise exactly-once processing when the consumer writes to an outside database?
questions.a: Because broker clocks drift, so duplicate delivery is impossible to detect
questions.b: Because exactly-once semantics require a replication factor larger than most production clusters are willing to run anyway
questions.c: The commit to the database and the acknowledgment to the broker are two writes with a crash window between them
questions.d: Because consumers cannot hold a message long enough for the broker to record it
questions.explanation: Two systems, two logs, no shared atomic commit, so either the effect lands twice or the acknowledgment does. Option B sounds technical but treats durability configuration as a solution to that gap.

questions.text: A queue's visibility timeout is much shorter than the handler's typical duration. What follows?
questions.a: Messages are simply lost, because the broker deletes any message whose timeout elapses before acknowledgment
questions.b: The message becomes visible again and a second consumer works on it while the first is still working
questions.c: Consumers stop prefetching, which silently reduces throughput across the whole fleet
questions.d: The broker extends the timeout automatically for long-running handlers
questions.explanation: The visibility lease expires mid-work, so the same message is handed to another consumer and both proceed. Option A is the opposite failure, belonging to at-most-once configurations rather than this one.

questions.text: What is a dead-letter queue for?
questions.a: Holding messages that failed repeatedly so they stop blocking the healthy ones
questions.b: Storing the messages that no consumer has claimed yet while a deployment is scaling the fleet back up again
questions.c: Recording every message the broker has ever delivered, for audit
questions.d: Buffering traffic during a planned deployment so nothing is processed twice
questions.explanation: It parks poison messages out of the critical path with their attempt history attached, so one bad record cannot stall a partition. Option B describes ordinary queue backlog, which is a different alarm entirely.

questions.text: Events for one aggregate must be applied in arrival order while the rest of the fleet stays parallel. What gives that?
questions.a: Running a single consumer process for the entire topic, which is the only way to guarantee global ordering reliably
questions.b: Sorting by event timestamp inside the handler before applying anything
questions.c: Locking the aggregate row for the duration of every handler invocation
questions.d: Partitioning the key by aggregate id, so order holds inside a partition and nothing is promised across partitions
questions.explanation: Ordering is a property of the unit of parallelism, so grouping by identifier orders what matters and keeps unrelated work concurrent. Option A buys order at the throughput of one consumer, which is the usual dead end.

questions.text: What does a transactional outbox make atomic that publishing after commit does not?
questions.a: The consumer's acknowledgment and the removal of the message from the broker's durable log are made into one operation
questions.b: The cache entry and the database row for the same aggregate
questions.c: The state change and the record that the event must be published, so neither can exist without the other
questions.d: The publish call and the subscriber's processing of that publish
questions.explanation: Writing the event in the same transaction as the state removes the crash window where one landed and the other did not. Option D reaches into the subscriber, whose processing the outbox cannot control at all.

questions.text: In a service-oriented design, what does it mean for one service to own a dataset?
questions.a: Every service may write it as long as it records the change in its own log
questions.b: The dataset lives in a shared schema that the platform team maintains centrally for everyone
questions.c: One service is the only writer and everything else goes through its interface
questions.d: Ownership is a code label in the repository that decides who reviews pull requests
questions.explanation: Single-writer ownership is what makes the schema a private detail and the interface a promise. Option A is the distributed audit fallacy: recording a write somewhere else does not make it coordinated.

questions.text: A table sharded by region shows one shard near saturation while the others idle. Which property of the key explains it?
questions.a: The key has too many distinct values for the cluster to hash evenly
questions.b: Low cardinality combined with skewed traffic concentrates a large share of writes into a few shards
questions.c: The key is monotonically increasing, which always forces a right-edge hotspot
questions.d: Region is not indexable in most engines, so every write turns into a broadcast that all shards must answer
questions.explanation: Few possible values and uneven demand mean some shards carry far more keys than others. Option C is the other classic hotspot story, but a region value is not increasing, which is why it does not fit here.

questions.text: Reads mostly filter by tenant while writes arrive keyed by device event. What goes wrong when the table is sharded on event time?
questions.a: Writes hot-spot on the newest shard while reads are unaffected, because event time is indexed on every shard
questions.b: Nothing, because the router hashes the time key so that it spreads evenly across all shards
questions.c: The cluster has to be rebalanced every time a new tenant is created
questions.d: Tenant reads cannot name the shard key, so they broadcast to every shard and pay the cluster size
questions.explanation: A query that does not mention the shard key cannot be routed, so it fans out and merges everywhere. Option A is the half-truth: the write hot-spot is real, but the read broadcast is the bigger structural cost.

questions.text: Why is a plain increasing integer primary key awkward in a high-write distributed table?
questions.a: Every insert lands on the same edge of the same structure, concentrating writes and leaking volume
questions.b: Distributed engines cannot guarantee uniqueness, so identifiers collide constantly
questions.c: Integer primary keys cannot be used as foreign keys once the related data is partitioned across shards
questions.d: Increasing keys prevent any form of cursor pagination on large tables
questions.explanation: Monotonic values pile inserts onto one hot region and advertise business volume to anyone who reads an id. Option C sounds like a rule but is not one; partitioned stores tolerate integer foreign keys just fine.

questions.text: A projection must be rebuilt after a logic change while live events keep arriving. What must the rebuild respect?
questions.a: The wall-clock time at which each event was generated, so that history is always applied in true temporal order
questions.b: The order the build system produced, since replay always follows deployment order
questions.c: Event sequence numbers, so that replayed older state cannot overwrite newer state written live
questions.d: Nothing beyond the checkpoint, because the projection is deterministic by construction
questions.explanation: Backfill and live writes race, and only a monotonic per-aggregate sequence says which state is newer. Option A is the appealing mistake: clocks drift and event time is not generation time.

questions.text: Two services read and write the same database table. What is the main cost of that arrangement?
questions.a: Connection pools have to be shared, which caps the throughput of both services
questions.b: Any schema change becomes a coordinated deployment, because both writers must agree on the shape
questions.c: A relational database cannot enforce foreign keys when two different services own the writes, so integrity is gone
questions.d: It prevents either service from having its own health check or metrics dashboard
questions.explanation: A shared table couples release ordering and rollback for teams that were supposed to be independent. Option C is wrong in both halves: constraints still fire, and the real cost is the coordination, not the keys.

questions.text: What is a timeout on an outbound dependency call really protecting?
questions.a: The dependency, from receiving requests it cannot answer quickly
questions.b: Your own threads, connections and pool slots from being held while the remote side is slow
questions.c: The calling client, from ever receiving a response that arrives later than the user was willing to wait
questions.d: The load balancer, from routing traffic to an unhealthy instance
questions.explanation: The cost of a slow dependency is capacity you keep spending on it, which is what the timeout caps. Option C describes user patience, which is the caller's deadline rather than this call's budget.

questions.text: During a partial outage every client retries a failed request once, and the outage deepens. What is the arithmetic cause?
questions.a: Retries travel through a separate code path that bypasses the connection pool and so consumes fresh sockets for every attempt
questions.b: The load balancer prefers instances that already have queued requests
questions.c: Timeouts release resources more slowly than successful responses do
questions.d: Retried traffic roughly doubles the offered load while capacity is already reduced, and the failures were slow ones
questions.explanation: A failure rate plus one retry multiplies load precisely when there is no headroom, which is a feedback loop rather than a mitigation. Option C is partly true and beside the point: the multiplier, not the release rate, deepens the outage.

questions.text: A fleet of clients all uses exponential backoff and still arrives in unison against a recovering dependency. What is missing?
questions.a: Jitter and a retry budget, because synchronized failure produces synchronized wake-up times
questions.b: A larger base delay, since the exponential term dominates everything else
questions.c: A circuit breaker on the dependency, which would remove the retries entirely
questions.d: Longer health check intervals, because the dependency needs more warm-up time before any client is allowed to return
questions.explanation: Without randomization, clients that failed together retry together on the same schedule, and without a budget the retries outscale the original traffic. Option B increases the delay while keeping the herd aligned.

questions.text: While a circuit breaker is open, what is the caller expected to do?
questions.a: Wait until the dependency answers so the request is not lost
questions.b: Keep retrying the same call at a lower scheduling priority until the breaker decides to close on its own
questions.c: Use a fallback: cached data, a reduced feature, or an honest error the user can act on
questions.d: Nothing, because the breaker replays the request when it closes again
questions.explanation: The breaker only decides how fast failure happens; the value it protects is whatever the caller substitutes instead. Option D imagines stored replay, which no ordinary breaker performs.

questions.text: One dependency slows to two seconds and unrelated endpoints on the same service begin timing out. What is the mechanism?
questions.a: Slow responses consume more bandwidth, starving the other endpoints of throughput
questions.b: A shared connection or thread pool is occupied by the slow calls, so unrelated work has nothing to run on
questions.c: The balancer declares the whole instance unhealthy and drains every in-flight request from it at the same moment
questions.d: Metric collection slows down under long requests and hides the real cause
questions.explanation: Waiting is a resource, and a single shared pool makes every dependency share one failure domain. Option A reaches for bandwidth, which is rarely the constraint in this shape of outage.

questions.text: What does splitting pools and concurrency limits per dependency trade away?
questions.a: Visibility, because per-dependency limits cannot be exported as metrics
questions.b: Idempotency, since a bounded pool rejects requests that were already recorded
questions.c: Latency, because a per-dependency pool inserts one more queueing step in front of every single outbound call the service makes
questions.d: Some peak throughput, since a limit that protects one dependency may refuse work the system could have absorbed
questions.explanation: Isolation bounds damage by refusing to let a healthy dependency borrow capacity from a broken one. Option C is the intuitive objection, but the extra queue is exactly what makes waiting visible instead of fatal.

questions.text: An authorization service behind your API becomes unreachable. What should decide whether you fail open or closed?
questions.a: What the check protects and how long it can plausibly be unavailable, written down before the incident
questions.b: The client library's default, because a well-vetted library already encodes the correct policy for your threat model
questions.c: Always fail open, because availability is the only signal users can perceive
questions.d: Always fail closed, since any request that passes without a check is a breach
questions.explanation: The choice is a business judgement about which failure is worse, and it needs a named owner rather than a reflex. Options C and D are the two absolutes people reach for, and both are wrong for some endpoint somewhere.

questions.text: What does a distributed trace provide that metrics and logs alone do not?
questions.a: A permanent record of every value the service read from the database during the request's lifetime
questions.b: A way to alert on error rates before users notice them at all
questions.c: Which hop in a chain of calls consumed the time for one specific request
questions.d: Structured log lines without needing to instrument any code by hand
questions.explanation: A trace attributes one request latency across the calls it made, which aggregates and per-service logs cannot reconstruct. Option A overstates it: traces record spans and timings, not application data.

questions.text: Why does head-based sampling systematically hide the slowest requests?
questions.a: Slow requests are usually dropped by the collector, because its buffer overflows before their spans can be encoded
questions.b: The sampling decision is taken before the outcome is known, so rare slow traces are not preferentially kept
questions.c: Head sampling only records errors, and a slow request is not an error
questions.d: Slow requests produce fewer spans, so they are undercounted in every sample
questions.explanation: Deciding at entry means the interesting one-in-a-hundred request is discarded with the ordinary ones, which is why tail-based sampling exists. Option C inverts the behaviour: error-focused retention is a feature of tail decisions.

questions.text: A latency histogram gains a label carrying the user id. What is the likely consequence?
questions.a: Percentile accuracy degrades badly, because each individual series ends up holding far fewer observations to work with
questions.b: Nothing serious, since labels are stored as pointers rather than copied
questions.c: The collector compresses the extra series, so only storage cost rises
questions.d: Series count multiplies with users, which can overwhelm the metrics store and the queries running against it
questions.explanation: High-cardinality labels explode the number of time series, which is the cost driver and the failure mode of a metrics backend. Option A is a plausible statistics story, but the real damage is operational scale rather than accuracy.

questions.text: A closed-loop load test reports flat throughput with steadily rising latency. What does that actually show?
questions.a: Offered load fell as responses slowed, so the run measures concurrency rather than a capacity ceiling
questions.b: The system has clearly reached its true throughput ceiling, so the figure can be used for capacity planning directly
questions.c: The generator is the bottleneck, which is proven by the flat throughput line
questions.d: Latency and throughput are unrelated, so both curves can be read separately
questions.explanation: In a closed loop the virtual users wait, so slowing the system silently reduces the pressure being applied. Option B is the misreading that fills capacity plans with a number from a concurrency setting.

questions.text: Which measurement most effectively turns cost into a constraint engineers act on?
questions.a: Total monthly spend from the invoice, reported for the entire organization at the start of each quarter
questions.b: Cost per unit of product, because it exposes per-request work that grew silently across releases
questions.c: The percentage of instances using spot capacity during off-peak hours
questions.d: A comparison of your provider's prices with a competitor's published list
questions.explanation: A per-unit figure moves when a design decision moves, so it lands in code review rather than in a finance report. Option A is real money but unattributable, which is why it changes no engineering behaviour.
